# The expert founders: what changed in v1.1.0

From v1.0.0 (2026-10-15, `a41cf8745`) to v1.1.0 (2026-10-15, this release), paragraph by paragraph.

2 paragraphs added, 1 removed, 3 changed in place, 45 unchanged. About 47 words added and 19 removed. Insertions are marked like this, deletions like this; unchanged runs are folded to one line; figures appear as their file names.

[all versions](../the-expert-founders.md)

1 unchanged paragraph

Summary: For twenty years the winning technology startup was usually built by a clever, ambitious outsider: someone who found a pain point, often through a hundred conversations with people they could reach, raised money on belief, hired the subject-matter experts, and displaced incumbents that had the customers, the knowledge and sometimes the money. It is a very American playbook, many bets for a few large wins, and it changed whole industries. It also has a second act: the disruptors became the incumbents, and much of what they built is now the software everyone complains about. My argument is that generative AI changes who can start. When agents do most of the execution, the people who know the problem can build the product themselves, without the millions that used to come first. The data on experts was always on their side: the fastest-growing US startups are founded at a mean age of 45, and three or more years in the same industry doubles the rate of top-tier success. And this favours Europe: its investors want to see it working, value lower, and ask for more revenue at the raise, which is exactly the discipline an expert founder needs, because money too early is one of the most reliable ways to kill a startup. Three examples: me in security, a knee surgeon in knee health, and a foundertranscriber in legal records.transcription.
